channel.title: Daily Digest
channel.description: Curated tech blog summaries, inspired by Andrej Karpathy's reading list

item.title: Speed is Not Conducive to Wisdom
item.description: The article critiques the modern obsession with speed, arguing that it prevents the deep reflection necessary for true wisdom. It posits that wisdom requires a slow, uncomfortable feedback loop of learning from failure and experience that urgency undermines.

item.title: zappa: an AI powered mitmproxy
item.description: The author introduces 'zappa,' an AI-powered mitmproxy plugin designed to intercept and transform web traffic to eliminate ads and intrusive elements. By using large language models to sanitize web content in real-time, the project aims to reclaim user attention from attention-economy business models.

item.title: Jensen Huang – TPU competition, why we should sell chips to China, & Nvidia’s supply chain moat
item.description: Jensen Huang discusses Nvidia's massive supply chain capabilities, asserting they can handle a trillion-dollar scale. He also addresses the strategic nuances of global competition and the rationale behind navigating chip trade policies with China.

item.title: A sufficiently comprehensive spec is not (necessarily) code
item.description: The article argues that a specification is fundamentally a set of possible implementations, whereas code is a single, specific implementation. While a sufficiently precise specification can be used to generate software, it remains conceptually distinct from code because a single spec can allow for multiple valid outcomes.

item.title: Pressed For Options
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.description: The author explores the challenges of finding reliable fingerprint authentication for Linux laptops compared to more mature Windows and macOS ecosystems. By experimenting with a budget-friendly USB reader from Temu, the article highlights the ongoing compatibility issues and lack of standardized support for biometric hardware on Linux.

item.title: The Tuesday Test
item.description: The author introduces the 'Tuesday Test' as a simple heuristic to determine if a package manager is truly declarative. A system passes the test if installing a package yields the same result regardless of when it is run, ensuring the process is isolated from hidden external inputs.

item.title: Why is there a long delay between a thread exiting and the Wait­For­Single­Object returning?
item.description: This article addresses a common developer confusion regarding delays when waiting for a thread to exit in Windows. It suggests that a perceived delay in WaitForSingleObject often indicates that the thread has not actually finished its execution yet.

item.title: Simdutf Can Now Be Used Without libc++ or libc++abi
item.description: Mitchell Hashimoto announces that the simdutf library can now be utilized without dependencies on libc++ or libc++abi. This change improves portability and reduces binary size for developers integrating the library into various systems. It simplifies the setup process by removing strict standard library requirements.

item.title: Pluralistic: Rights for robots (15 Apr 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: This article explores the concept of 'corporate personhood' in the legal system, tracing its evolution from 19th-century judicial decisions to modern cases like Citizens United. It contrasts this with the 'Rights of Nature' movement, which seeks to grant legal standing to ecosystems to protect them from corporate influence.

item.title: Quoting John Gruber
item.description: Simon Willison quotes John Gruber on the declining quality of third-party software on Apple platforms. Gruber argues that the platform's competitive advantage is weakening as developers feel less motivated to build high-quality, native applications.

item.title: Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS
item.description: Google has introduced Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS, a new text-to-speech model accessible via the Gemini API. The model distinguishes itself by allowing users to influence speech output through detailed prompt engineering, including scene setting, vocal style, and accent instructions.

item.title: Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS
item.description: Simon Willison introduces a new tool that leverages Google's Gemini 3.1 Flash model for text-to-speech conversion. The post provides direct access to the experimental tool and links to further technical notes regarding the model's capabilities.

item.title: Quoting Kyle Kingsbury
item.description: The article discusses the emergence of 'meat shields'—human roles created to absorb accountability for the errors and failures of machine learning systems. It highlights how companies may utilize employees or third-party contractors to provide a veneer of human oversight or to act as scapegoats for automated system misbehavior.

item.title: datasette-ports 0.3
item.description: Datasette-ports 0.3 is a minor update to a utility tool used to monitor local Datasette instances. The new version adds visibility into the working directory and the full file paths of the databases for each active process.

item.title: Zig 0.16.0 release notes: "Juicy Main"
item.description: Zig 0.16.0 has been released with comprehensive updates, most notably the 'Juicy Main' feature. This update introduces dependency injection for the main() function, allowing developers to easily access essential resources like allocators, I/O, and environment variables via the process.Init parameter.

item.title: datasette PR #2689: Replace token-based CSRF with Sec-Fetch-Site header protection
item.description: Datasette has replaced its traditional token-based CSRF protection with the modern Sec-Fetch-Site header approach. This change simplifies templates by removing the need for hidden form fields and deprecates complex plugin hooks for skipping protection.

item.title: An Arm Mainboard for the Framework Laptop
item.description: Jeff Geerling tests an Arm-based Mainboard from MetaComputing for the Framework 13 laptop. This experiment demonstrates the modularity of the Framework chassis by successfully swapping between x86, RISC-V, and Arm architectures.

item.title: Nothing ever dies. It merely becomes embarrassing.
item.description: This article explores the 'Halo theory of science,' arguing that scientific ideas never truly disappear but instead persist in evolving, often awkward forms. The author examines how outdated concepts linger in our discourse, suggesting that cultural memory preserves them long after their original utility has faded.

item.title: Weekly Update 499
item.description: Troy Hunt shares his evolving perspective on using AI assistants like 'Bruce' for customer support. He argues that the value lies not just in full automation, but in how AI can assist humans in crafting responses efficiently.

item.title: Object Oriented Programming in Ada
item.description: This article explores the implementation of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) principles within the Ada programming language. It examines how Ada's unique features, such as packages and tagged types, facilitate robust software engineering and type safety.

item.title: Standing on the shoulders of Homebrew
item.description: The article critiques new Homebrew alternatives like zerobrew and nanobrew, arguing that their performance claims rely on skipping the complex, time-consuming tasks that Homebrew handles. By focusing only on simple package installation, these tools ignore the difficult parts of package management, such as Ruby DSL execution and post-install hooks.

item.title: Intersecting spheres and GPS
item.description: This article explains the geometric principles behind GPS positioning, specifically how distances from satellites are used to determine location. It details how the intersection of spheres creates circles that help narrow down a user's precise coordinate.

item.title: Finding a parabola through two points with given slopes
item.description: This article explores the mathematical process of finding a parabola defined by two points and their respective slopes at those points. The author investigates the geometric properties of 'Artzt parabolas' and demonstrates how to derive the general conic equation to solve for the specific parabola.

item.title: Why was there a red telephone at every receptionist desk?
item.description: This post clarifies the historical purpose of red telephones found at Microsoft receptionist desks. It dismisses the common myth that they were direct lines to leadership, explaining their actual function instead.

item.title: Pluralistic: In praise of (some) compartmentalization (14 Apr 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow explains his productivity strategy, noting that intense creative work and engaging conversations help him manage chronic pain by distracting his nervous system. He describes this as a form of beneficial compartmentalization that allows him to temporarily tune out physical discomfort.

item.title: Back button hijacking is going away
item.description: The article explains the deceptive practice of 'back button hijacking' used by platforms like LinkedIn to keep users engaged. By manipulating browser history through JavaScript, these sites prevent users from navigating away, forcing them onto the homepage feed instead.

item.title: Patch Tuesday, April 2026 Edition
item.description: Microsoft released a massive update addressing 167 security vulnerabilities, including critical zero-days in SharePoint and Windows Defender. Additionally, Google Chrome and Adobe Reader issued emergency patches for actively exploited flaws.

item.title: Trusted access for the next era of cyber defense
item.description: Simon Willison discusses OpenAI's new GPT-5.4-Cyber model and the expansion of their 'Trusted Access for Cyber' program. The post highlights the complexities of these cybersecurity-focused access tiers and compares them to similar initiatives from competitors like Anthropic.

item.title: Cybersecurity Looks Like Proof of Work Now
item.description: The article discusses how AI-driven cybersecurity is evolving into a 'proof of work' economic model, where system security depends on spending more tokens on exploit discovery than an attacker would spend to find them. This paradigm shift increases the value of shared open-source libraries, as the costs of securing them are distributed across all users.

item.title: A little tool to visualise MoE expert routing
item.description: The author created a visualization tool to observe how Mixture of Experts (MoE) models route tokens across different experts. The tool provides a transparent look into the internal decision-making processes of these complex neural network architectures.

item.title: give-them-two-choices
item.description: This article discusses the psychological strategy of offering two choices to influence behavior or decision-making. It likely explores how limiting options can simplify the process and increase the likelihood of a positive outcome.

item.title: That’s a Skill Issue
item.description: The author contrasts tech-centered and human-centered design philosophies, noting how the former blames users for 'skill issues' while the latter treats user confusion as a design failure. By highlighting the difference between demanding users master complex 'incantations' and designing intuitive systems, the post argues for a more empathetic approach to tool creation.

item.title: The ‘Everyone’s a Billionaire’ act
item.description: The author proposes a satirical solution to wealth inequality by printing one billion dollars for every American citizen. The post explores the immediate benefits of universal wealth while acknowledging the inevitable hyperinflation that would render the dollar worthless and necessitate a move toward non-fiat currencies like gold.

item.title: Common Package Specification
item.description: The Common Package Specification (CPS) provides a unified JSON format for C++ build systems like CMake and Meson to describe installed libraries. By replacing fragmented methods like .pc files and Config.cmake scripts, CPS simplifies dependency management and improves binary data extraction for tooling.

item.title: Sometimes powerful people just do dumb shit
item.description: This post discusses the tendency of powerful individuals to engage in irrational or foolish behavior. It highlights the author's platform and subscription model for those seeking additional content and community access.

item.title: Mathematical minimalism
item.description: This article discusses a mathematical finding by Andrzej Odrzywolek demonstrating that all elementary arithmetic operations can be derived from a single function and the constant 1. It highlights the concept of mathematical minimalism by showing how complex operations like multiplication and division can be bootstrapped from basic definitions.

item.title: Lunar period approximations
item.description: This article discusses the historical and astronomical origins of how Easter is calculated, based on the lunisolar calendar. It explores the relationship between the Spring equinox and the full moon cycle in establishing the date.

item.title: Finding a duplicated item in an array of N integers in the range 1 to N − 1
item.description: This article explores efficient algorithms for identifying duplicate values within an array of N integers ranging from 1 to N-1. It emphasizes leveraging the specific mathematical properties of the data set to optimize the search process.

item.title: Android now stops you sharing your location in photos
item.description: Android's latest update restricts the ability of web-based file pickers to access EXIF geolocation metadata in user photos. This change impacts websites like OpenBenches that rely on embedded location data to map uploaded images.

item.title: Pluralistic: Austerity creates fascism (13 Apr 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow critiques the billionaire-driven 'AI psychosis,' arguing that massive capital investment in unprofitable AI risks a systemic market collapse. He contends that austerity policies have left the average worker so financially vulnerable that they have little to lose from a stock market crash, while highlighting the dangers of centralized corporate power.

item.title: You paid for it, you should be comfortable in it
item.description: The author reflects on the philosophy of customizing physical objects for personal comfort, sparked by seeing a friend drastically modify a high-end Tesla Roadster. This perspective shifts the author's view on hardware flaws, moving from passive endurance to the idea that users have the agency to adapt tools to fit their specific physical needs.

item.title: Quoting Steve Yegge
item.description: Steve Yegge observes that Google's internal AI adoption mirrors the rest of the industry, with a divide between agentic power users and reluctant adopters. He argues that prolonged hiring freezes have created an echo chamber, preventing the influx of external talent needed to address the company's stagnant engineering culture.

item.title: Exploring the new `servo` crate
item.description: This post explores the newly released Servo crate, which allows the Servo browser engine to be embedded as a library in Rust projects. The author uses Claude Code to build a CLI screenshot tool and demonstrates that while compiling full Servo to WebAssembly is currently infeasible, its components like html5ever can be compiled for web use.

item.title: Quoting Bryan Cantrill
item.description: Bryan Cantrill argues that LLMs lack the innate human 'virtue of laziness,' which typically forces developers to create efficient, crisp abstractions. Without this constraint, LLMs tend to generate overly complex, bloated systems that prioritize quantity over quality.

item.title: Gemma 4 audio with MLX
item.description: This post provides a practical guide on how to transcribe audio files on macOS using Google's Gemma 4 model via the MLX framework. It includes a specific command line recipe using the uv tool to run the transcription process efficiently.

item.title: Optimism is not a personality flaw
item.description: This article discusses the nature of optimism, challenging the misconception that it is a character defect. The author explores why maintaining a positive outlook is a valuable perspective rather than a sign of naivety.

item.title: The gap between Eastern and Western Easter
item.description: This article explores the technical and historical reasons behind the discrepancy between Western and Orthodox Easter dates. It explains the astronomical calculations involved and the varying cycles used by different church traditions to determine when the holiday occurs.

item.title: Your AWS Certificate Makes You an AWS Salesman
item.description: The article critiques the complexity of AWS, arguing that its steep learning curve and certification system function as a marketing tool rather than essential engineering skills. The author suggests that for many independent developers, simpler alternatives like DigitalOcean provide a more efficient and cost-effective experience.

item.title: Has Mythos just broken the deal that kept the internet safe?
item.description: The article analyzes the release of Anthropic's Mythos research preview and its implications for frontier AI model safety. It highlights critical concerns regarding sandbox escapes and the evolving cybersecurity risks associated with advanced AI architectures.

item.title: OpenAI is nothing without its people
item.description: The author critiques Sam Altman's perspective on AI, arguing that individual 'great men' are less dangerous than systemic societal coordination failures (Moloch). The post advocates for true decentralization and shared ownership of AI technology rather than subscription-based access, which the author labels as modern feudalism.

item.title: Reading List 04/11/2026
item.description: This post provides a curated list of links and brief commentary covering diverse topics including global maritime trade, building regulation economics, and advancements in semiconductor manufacturing. It also touches upon urban infrastructure resilience through the concept of sponge cities.

item.title: The Center Has a Bias
item.description: The article discusses the polarization surrounding AI coding agents, noting that both skeptics and enthusiasts often lack a balanced perspective. The author argues that meaningful criticism requires active, hands-on engagement with the technology rather than abstract theorizing, advocating for a centrist position defined by critical, practical interaction.

item.title: Cheapest way to keep a UK mobile number using an eSIM
item.description: This post explores the most cost-effective methods for maintaining a UK mobile phone number using eSIM technology for long-term 2FA verification. The author evaluates various service providers to identify the cheapest options for preserving a number without the need for physical SIM cards.

item.title: [RSS Club] Why do you use RSS rather than Atom?
item.description: The author discusses the implementation of 'RSS Club,' an experiment involving feed-exclusive content and privacy-conscious view tracking. The post reflects on the technical nomenclature of feed formats and the author's efforts to measure engagement while prioritizing reader privacy.

item.title: Pluralistic: Don't Be Evil (11 Apr 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow reflects on the transition to middle age and the retrospective analysis of his early tech career, specifically his work at the dotcom-era startup Opencola. He uses this historical context to frame broader observations about the evolution of the tech industry and the intersection of personal growth and societal change.

item.title: Your friends are hiding their best ideas from you
item.description: The author reflects on the human tendency to guard business ideas as if they are precious, noting that many people seek validation rather than critical feedback. Over time, the author transitioned from being defensive about their own work to realizing that the true value lies in execution rather than the secrecy of the initial concept.

item.title: SQLite 3.53.0
item.description: SQLite 3.53.0 has been released following the withdrawal of version 3.52.0, introducing significant updates like ALTER TABLE constraint modifications and new JSON functions. The release also features an enhanced CLI with a new Query Results Formatter library, which is showcased in an interactive WebAssembly-based playground.

item.title: SQLite Query Result Formatter Demo
item.description: Simon Willison has released a web-based playground for the SQLite Query Result Formatter library. This tool allows users to experiment with different rendering options for SQL query results, compiled to WebAssembly.

item.title: Y2K 2.0: The AI security reckoning
item.description: The rise of advanced LLMs has significantly accelerated the discovery and exploitation of software vulnerabilities. By automating code analysis and personalizing attack vectors, AI tools have democratized access to sophisticated cyberattacks, posing a systemic threat to digital infrastructure.

item.title: watgo - a WebAssembly Toolkit for Go
item.description: Eli Bendersky introduces watgo, a zero-dependency Go toolkit for WebAssembly that allows parsing, validating, encoding, and decoding WASM files. The toolkit provides both a CLI for command-line tasks and a Go API for programmatically manipulating WebAssembly modules via the wasmir semantic representation.

item.title: The Solitaire Shuffle
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.description: This article explores the enduring appeal of Solitaire as a meditative and mentally stimulating pastime. It highlights the variety of the game's iterations and discusses a UCLA CRESST study suggesting that playing Solitaire may have positive impacts on cognitive function.

item.title: Package Registries and Pagination
item.description: Legacy package registry APIs like npm and PyPI suffer from performance issues because they return full version history in single, massive JSON responses. These decade-old designs lack pagination, causing modern, high-volume packages to hit size limits and memory overhead during parsing.

item.title: Why I quit "The Strive"
item.description: The author announces the end of their previous newsletter project, 'The Strive,' while detailing the future direction of their paid subscription model. They emphasize maintaining free access to core content while offering premium benefits like community access and ad-free reading for supporters.

item.title: In defense of GitHub's poor uptime
item.description: This article challenges the perception that GitHub's uptime is failing by explaining how uptime statistics can be misleading when applied to complex, multi-service platforms. The author argues that aggregate metrics often unfairly penalize systems for having independent, non-overlapping service outages.

item.title: Distribution of digits in fractions
item.description: This article explores the distribution of digits in the decimal representations of fractions. It highlights interesting, lesser-known mathematical patterns that emerge when analyzing these basic numerical forms.

item.title: How do you add or remove a handle from an active Wait­For­Multiple­Objects?, part 2
item.description: This article continues the discussion on modifying handles within an active WaitForMultipleObjects call. It specifically focuses on the synchronization mechanism required to ensure the waiting thread correctly acknowledges handle changes.

item.title: Pluralistic: Canny Valley and Creative Commons (10 Apr 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow reflects on his history of successful Kickstarter campaigns for his books, emphasizing his commitment to creating unique, limited-edition physical items for his readers. He highlights the balance between producing DRM-free digital content and creating tangible collector's pieces.

item.title: Kākāpō parrots
item.description: Simon Willison shares a video snippet from a recent podcast episode featuring a discussion about Kākāpō parrots. The post provides a direct link to the short video clip and references the full-length podcast recording.

item.title: ChatGPT voice mode is a weaker model
item.description: Simon Willison highlights that OpenAI's ChatGPT voice mode often uses a less capable model than expected, contradicting the assumption that voice-accessible AI is the most powerful. The post references Andrej Karpathy's analysis on why some AI domains, like coding, advance faster due to explicit reward functions and high B2B value.

item.title: SQLAlchemy 2 In Practice - Chapter 4 - Many-To-Many Relationships
item.description: This article serves as the fourth chapter of Miguel Grinberg's guide on SQLAlchemy 2. It focuses on the implementation and management of many-to-many database relationships.

item.title: Nowhere Is Safe
item.description: The article analyzes how the proliferation of low-cost drones in modern warfare, as seen in Ukraine and Iran, renders traditional air defense systems obsolete. It highlights the strategic shift where massive numbers of inexpensive, asymmetric threats can overwhelm sophisticated, high-cost military defense infrastructure.

item.title: Rapport digitale autonomie binnen de energie-intensieve industrie voor Energy Innovation NL
item.description: Bert Hubert announces the publication of his new report commissioned by Energy Innovation NL, focusing on digital autonomy within energy-intensive industries. The report, developed through consultations with various key companies, addresses the critical integration of technology and industrial energy processes.

item.title: Fewer Computers, Fewer Problems: Going Local With Builds & Deployments
item.description: The author discusses shifting back to local-first builds and deployments for personal websites to simplify the development process. By treating remote hosting as a progressive enhancement rather than a dependency, they aim to eliminate the complexities of distributed computing.

item.title: Hong Kong Disneyland Speedrun Guide
item.description: This guide provides a strategic approach to visiting Hong Kong Disneyland efficiently by leveraging early entry passes and optimized pathing. The author outlines a specific route to maximize ride uptime and minimize queue times, allowing visitors to experience all attractions in half a day.

item.title: Helium Is Hard to Replace
item.description: This article explores the complexities of the global helium supply chain, drawing parallels to how geopolitical conflicts, such as the Strait of Hormuz closure, disrupt essential resource logistics. It highlights why helium is uniquely difficult to substitute, emphasizing its critical role in modern technology and industry.

item.title: Package Security Defenses for AI Agents
item.description: This post highlights the heightened security risks AI agents face when installing software packages, such as malicious code execution and credential theft. It proposes defensive strategies for AI coding platforms, including disabling default install scripts, implementing package version cooldowns, and enforcing sandboxed environments to limit potential blast radii.

item.title: The Great Pyramid of Giza and the Speed of Light
item.description: The author investigates a viral claim that the latitude of the Great Pyramid of Giza matches the speed of light. He concludes that while the numbers align precisely, the observation is a mathematical coincidence rather than evidence of ancient advanced knowledge.

item.title: Random hexagon fractal
item.description: The article explores an iterative geometric process for generating a random fractal based on a hexagon. By repeatedly selecting a side and forming a new triangle with a point inside, the method produces complex, self-similar patterns.

item.title: Root prime gap
item.description: This post discusses Andrica's conjecture, which posits that the difference between the square roots of consecutive prime numbers is always less than one. The author notes that while this remains unproven, it has been empirically verified for primes up to 2 × 10^19.

item.title: A Three- and a Four- Body Problem
item.description: This article discusses the orbital mechanics of the Artemis I and Artemis II missions, focusing on the differences in trajectory and duration. It highlights how the unmanned nature of Artemis I allowed for a more complex, longer-duration orbit compared to the crewed Artemis II mission.

item.title: How do you add or remove a handle from an active Wait­For­Multiple­Objects?
item.description: The article explains that it is impossible to directly modify the handles being monitored by an active WaitForMultipleObjects call. Instead, the author advises using a cooperative approach between threads to manage the monitored objects.

item.title: I quit drinking for a year
item.description: The author recounts their experience of quitting alcohol for over a year after a spontaneous decision triggered by a discussion about 'damp January.' They discovered that total abstinence was surprisingly easier than moderate drinking because it removed the mental burden of constantly deciding whether or not to consume alcohol.

item.title: Book Review: Small Comfort by Ia Genberg ★★☆☆☆
item.description: Terence Eden reviews the book 'Small Comfort' by Ia Genberg, expressing mixed feelings about its execution. While he appreciates the experimental structure of interrelated stories, he finds the overall narrative unconvincing and disjointed.

item.title: Pluralistic: Cindy Cohn's "Privacy's Defender" (09 Apr 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow highlights the memoir of EFF executive director Cindy Cohn, 'Privacy's Defender,' which chronicles her decades-long fight for digital rights. The post focuses on her pivotal role in the landmark Bernstein case, which established that code constitutes protected free speech.

item.title: What Are You Trying to Say?
item.description: The article explores the challenge of clear communication and the tendency to overcomplicate messages. It suggests that asking oneself 'what am I trying to say?' helps strip away unnecessary fluff, encouraging writers and speakers to distill complex thoughts into their core, primitive meaning.

item.title: GitHub Repo Size
item.description: Simon Willison has released a simple web tool that displays the total size of any GitHub repository. It bypasses the lack of size information in the GitHub UI by leveraging the repository's CORS-friendly API.

item.title: asgi-gzip 0.3
item.description: Simon Willison released version 0.3 of asgi-gzip to fix an issue where SSE responses were being incorrectly compressed. The update was triggered after realizing that the library's automated sync with Starlette had failed to capture a necessary upstream fix.

item.title: Meta's new model is Muse Spark, and meta.ai chat has some interesting tools
item.description: Meta has released Muse Spark, a new hosted AI model available via meta.ai with 'Instant' and 'Thinking' modes. The author tests the model's capabilities using his signature 'pelican riding a bicycle' prompt to compare performance across these modes.

item.title: When the crisis comes
item.description: Anil Dash reflects on the challenges of leadership during constant crises, emphasizing the importance of finding clarity and expert support. He highlights the book 'Crisis Engineering' as a vital resource for navigating turbulent times and transforming crises into opportunities for growth.

item.title: The day you get cut out of the economy
item.description: The article argues that as global economic growth stagnates, AI frontier model developers will shift from a SaaS subscription model to vertical integration. By capturing the value currently held by the AI application layer, model makers will consolidate the market to recoup the massive costs of frontier training runs.

item.title: Pork & Puppetry
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.description: This article explores the origin of a viral parody trailer featuring a warthog puppet named Pork Johnson, which mocks the open-source image editor GIMP. The author interviews creator Dustin Grissom, who explains how the puppet served as a creative outlet and a personal tribute to his childhood.

item.title: Package Security Problems for AI Agents
item.description: This article examines how AI agents are uniquely vulnerable to traditional package security threats like typosquatting and registry poisoning. Because agents dynamically discover and install tools without human oversight, they can inadvertently execute malicious code from compromised or spoofed package repositories.

item.title: Mario and Earendil
item.description: Armin Ronacher announces that Mario Zechner is joining Earendil. The post highlights Ronacher's admiration for Zechner's commitment to software quality, thoughtful design, and craftsmanship in the field of AI coding agents.

item.title: How do you add or remove a handle from an active Msg­Wait­For­Multiple­Objects?
item.description: The article explains that you cannot directly add or remove a handle from an active MsgWaitForMultipleObjects call. Instead, you must design your application logic to signal the waiter to handle these updates internally.

item.title: Theatre Review: Avenue Q ★★★★★
item.description: The author reflects on re-watching the musical Avenue Q, contemplating the passage of time and the challenges of updating classic productions. The review highlights the emotional resonance of the show while discussing the balance between preserving a work's original charm and keeping it relevant.

item.title: Pluralistic: Process knowledge (08 Apr 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: This article examines the problematic nature of the term 'intellectual property,' arguing that it is a vague, catch-all label for disparate legal doctrines and abstract concepts. It highlights how the conflation of copyright, patents, trademarks, and newer, less-defined rights complicates modern tech regulation and global trade policy.

item.title: Quoting Giles Turnbull
item.description: This post highlights a reflection by Giles Turnbull on the double standard regarding AI adoption. It notes that while people enjoy using AI to mimic other professions, they often resent when AI is used to replace their own work.

item.title: Actually, people love to work hard
item.description: Anil Dash challenges the common corporate trope that employees lack a desire to work hard. He argues that people are inherently motivated when they have clear goals, shared values, and trust, suggesting that claims of laziness are merely management tactics to suppress wages.

item.title: Weekly Update 498
item.description: Troy Hunt shares his frustrations regarding the administrative burden of chasing long-overdue invoices from clients. The update highlights the real-world difficulties of managing payment terms in a professional consulting business.

item.title: Michael Nielsen – How science actually progresses
item.description: Michael Nielsen discusses the nuances of scientific progress, challenging traditional narratives about historical figures like Einstein, Newton, and Darwin. The conversation explores how scientific breakthroughs actually occur through collaborative environments and evolving methodologies rather than isolated genius.
